title: Spearman's Rank Correlation Analysis — spearman_rho
text: Spearman's rho measures strength direction monotonic relationship two variables. Unlike Pearson correlation, require linear relationship – just needs one variable consistently increase (decrease) increases. Think ranking data first, checking ranks tend go together. rho value ranges -1 +1: Strong positive (0.7 1.0): High ranks one variable go high ranks Moderate positive (0.3 0.7): Moderate tendency ranks increase together Weak positive (0 0.3): Slight tendency ranks increase together correlation (near 0): relationship variables Negative values: one variable's rank increases, 's tends decrease output also provides: p-value: Probability seeing correlation chance n: Number observation pairs used significance stars: Visual indicator (*** strong, ** strong, * moderate evidence)

title: Spearman's Rank Correlation Analysis — spearman_rho
text: Choose Spearman's rho : relationship monotonic necessarily linear data outliers (less impact ranks) variables ordinal (ordered categories) sure data meets Pearson correlation assumptions want detect monotonic trend, just linear ones

title: Spearman's Rank Correlation Analysis — spearman_rho
text: Spearman's rho usually larger magnitude Kendall's tau Spearman's rho better detecting linear relationships ranks Kendall's tau robust better statistical properties Spearman's rho commonly reported research

code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Basic correlation between two variables survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(life_satisfaction, political_orientation) #> Spearman Correlation: life_satisfaction x political_orientation #>   rho = -0.004, p = 0.833, N = 2228 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Correlation matrix for multiple variables survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(life_satisfaction, political_orientation, trust_media) #> Spearman Correlation: 3 variables #>   life_satisfaction x political_orientation: rho = -0.004, p = 0.833 #>   life_satisfaction x trust_media:           rho = 0.028, p = 0.181 #>   political_orientation x trust_media:       rho = 0.003, p = 0.885 #>   0/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 2177-2291 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Weights only filter cases (weight <= 0 or NA dropped); rho itself is # unweighted, matching SPSS NONPAR CORR survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(age, income, weights = sampling_weight) #> Spearman Correlation: age x income #>   rho = 0.003, p = 0.870, N = 2186 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Grouped correlations survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   spearman_rho(age, income, life_satisfaction) #> [region = East] #> Spearman Correlation: 3 variables #>   age x income:               rho = 0.058, p = 0.234 #>   age x life_satisfaction:    rho = -0.040, p = 0.391 #>   income x life_satisfaction: rho = 0.440, p < 0.001 *** #>   1/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 410-465 #> [region = West] #> Spearman Correlation: 3 variables #>   age x income:               rho = -0.008, p = 0.725 #>   age x life_satisfaction:    rho = -0.020, p = 0.382 #>   income x life_satisfaction: rho = 0.470, p < 0.001 *** #>   1/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 1705-1956 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Using tidyselect helpers survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(starts_with("trust"), weights = sampling_weight) #> Spearman Correlation: 3 variables #>   trust_government x trust_media:   rho = 0.008, p = 0.723 #>   trust_government x trust_science: rho = 0.027, p = 0.207 #>   trust_media x trust_science:      rho = 0.016, p = 0.453 #>   0/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 2227-2272 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Listwise deletion for missing data survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(age, income, use = "listwise") #> Spearman Correlation: age x income #>   rho = 0.003, p = 0.870, N = 2186 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # One-tailed test survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(age, income, alternative = "greater") #> Spearman Correlation: age x income [one-sided: greater] #>   rho = 0.003, p = 0.435, N = 2186 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # --- Three-layer output --- result <- spearman_rho(survey_data, age, income, life_satisfaction) result              # compact one-line overview #> Spearman Correlation: 3 variables #>   age x income:               rho = 0.003, p = 0.870 #>   age x life_satisfaction:    rho = -0.024, p = 0.238 #>   income x life_satisfaction: rho = 0.464, p < 0.001 *** #>   1/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 2115-2421 #> Use summary() for detailed output. summary(result)     # title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: Standardizes variables centering mean dividing measure spread. Supports multiple standardization methods including robust alternatives. used grouped data frame (via dplyr::group_by()), standardization performed within group.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
code: std(data, ..., method = "sd", weights = NULL, suffix = NULL, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data data frame numeric vector. ... Variables standardize (tidyselect). used data data frame. method Standardization method: "sd" Standard z-score: (x - mean) / sd (default) "2sd" Gelman's 2-SD method: (x - mean) / (2 * sd). Useful regression binary predictors. "mad" Robust: (x - median) / mad. Resistant outliers. "gmd" Gini's Mean Difference: (x - mean) / gmd. robust alternative. weights Optional survey weights. provided, weighted mean weighted SD used standardization. supported methods "sd" "2sd". Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. suffix character string appended column names (e.g., "_z"). NULL (default), original columns overwritten. na.rm Remove missing values computing mean SD? Default: TRUE.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data vector, standardized numeric vector. data data frame, modified data frame (invisibly).

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: sd (default): Standard z-transformation. Mean = 0, SD = 1. 2sd: Divides 2 standard deviations (Gelman, 2008). makes standardized continuous predictors comparable binary predictors regression. mad: Uses Median Absolute Deviation instead SD. Robust outliers. gmd: Uses Gini's Mean Difference — robust spread measure based pairwise absolute differences.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: weights provided, weighted mean weighted standard deviation (using SPSS frequency weight formula) used. supported methods "sd" "2sd". robust methods "mad" "gmd" support weights.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data grouped (via group_by()), standardization performed separately within group. useful within-group comparisons. Weights also subsetted per group.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: result plain numeric variable (value labels dropped, variable label kept " (standardized)" appended). Missing values imported data, including SPSS missing types, become plain NA – SPSS's DESCRIPTIVES /SAVE gives system-missing z-scores.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Standard z-scores data <- std(survey_data, age, income, suffix = "_z")  # Gelman 2-SD standardization (for regression) data <- std(survey_data, income, age, method = "2sd",             suffix = "_z")  # Robust standardization data <- std(survey_data, income, method = "mad", suffix = "_z")  # Weighted standardization data <- std(survey_data, income, age,             weights = sampling_weight, suffix = "_z")  # Group-wise standardization data <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   std(income, suffix = "_z")

text: t_test() helps determine two groups different average values. example, men women different satisfaction scores? Region spend Region B? year better last year? test tells : Whether difference statistically significant big difference (effect sizes) likely range true difference (confidence interval)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
code: t_test(   data,   ...,   group = NULL,   weights = NULL,   var.equal = FALSE,   mu = 0,   alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),   conf.level = 0.95 )

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... numeric variables test. List multiple variables use tidyselect helpers like starts_with("trust"). group variable defines two groups (e.g., gender, region). Must exactly two categories. Leave empty one-sample tests. weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. var.equal assume equal variances? (Default: FALSE) FALSE: Safer, works even groups vary differently (Welch's test) TRUE: Traditional approach, assumes equal spread (Student's test) mu Comparison value (Default: 0). two-sample tests, usually 0. one-sample tests, benchmark value. alternative Direction test: "two.sided" (default): difference "greater": First group higher "less": First group lower conf.level Confidence level intervals (Default: 0.95 = 95%)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Test results showing whether groups differ, including: t-statistic p-value statistical significance Mean difference confidence interval (one-sample tests: mean minus mu interval difference, SPSS One-Sample Test) Effect sizes (Cohen's d, Hedges' g, Glass' Delta) Group statistics (mean, SD, standard error mean, sample size) note column explains variable (group) computed, e.g. variance one group valid data Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections.

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: P-value: difference statistically significant? p < 0.001: strong evidence difference p < 0.01: Strong evidence difference p < 0.05: Moderate evidence difference p >= 0.05: significant difference found Effect Sizes (big difference?): Cohen's d: standard measure |d| < 0.2: Negligible difference |d| = 0.2-0.5: Small difference |d| = 0.5-0.8: Medium difference |d| > 0.8: Large difference Hedges' g: Corrected small samples Glass' Delta: Uses control group SD Confidence Interval: Range true difference likely falls includes 0, groups may differ Width indicates precision (narrower = precise)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Use t-test : exactly two groups compare outcome variable numeric (continuous) Groups independent (different people ) Data roughly normally distributed (n >= 30 per group) use : two groups (use ANOVA) Data severely skewed small samples (use Mann-Whitney) Groups paired/matched (use paired t-test - coming soon) Variables categorical (use chi-square)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: results show variance assumptions: Welch's test (var.equal = FALSE): Safer, assume equal variances Student's test (var.equal = TRUE): Traditional, assumes equal variances result t = 2.45, p = 0.015, d = 0.62 means: Groups 2.45 standard errors apart (t-statistic) 1.5% chance due random variation (p-value) Medium-sized practical difference (Cohen's d)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Always check sample sizes (aim 30+ per group) Consider statistical significance effect size Use weights population-level conclusions Plot data first check assumptions Report confidence intervals along p-values

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character
text: data data frame, tibble, single vector. ... (formals retained old names error clearly instead swallowed ....)

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: Creates 0/1 dummy variables categorical variables. Column names derived value labels available, making results readable SPSS-style data. Unlike model.matrix(), to_dummy() uses value labels column naming handles haven_labelled vectors correctly.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
code: to_dummy(data, ..., suffix = "val", ref = NULL, append = TRUE)

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: data data frame vector. data frame passed, use ... select variables. ... Variables dummy-code (tidyselect). used data data frame. suffix name dummy columns: "val" (default) uses raw value (e.g., gender_1), "label" uses value label (e.g., gender_Male). ref value use reference category (omitted output). NULL (default), categories get dummy variable. Set specific value n-1 coding (e.g., regression). factor, give level name (ref = "Male") number: original code to_label() factor, otherwise level position (ref = 1 = first level). ref matches category error. append TRUE (default), dummy columns appended original data frame. FALSE, dummy columns returned. Ignored data vector.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: append = TRUE (default), original data frame dummy columns appended. append = FALSE, tibble dummy columns. vector input, always tibble dummy columns.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: suffix = "val": {varname}_{value} (e.g., gender_1, gender_2). suffix = "label": {varname}_{label} labels cleaned (umlauts transliterated, e.g. "männlich" -> maennlich; spaces replaced _; special characters removed). Values without usable label (e.g. "..") use value; labels shared several values get value appended, every category keeps column.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: regression, typically need n-1 dummy variables. Set ref value reference category omit .

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Create dummies and append to data (default) data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender)  # Use labels for column names data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, suffix = "label")  # n-1 dummies with reference category data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, ref = 1)  # Multiple variables data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, education, suffix = "label")  # Return only the dummy columns (without original data) dummies <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, append = FALSE)

what: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: Converts haven_labelled variables factors, using value labels factor levels. primary function making labelled survey data ready plotting, cross-tabulation, regression analysis.

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
code: to_label(   data,   ...,   ordered = FALSE,   drop_na = TRUE,   drop_unused = FALSE,   add_non_labelled = FALSE,   drop.na = NULL,   drop.unused = NULL,   add.non.labelled = NULL )

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: data data frame, tibble, single vector. ... Optional: unquoted variable names (tidyselect supported). empty, converts every haven_labelled column whose values value-labelled; metric variables (e.g. age labels missing codes), weights partially labelled variables left unchanged message. Selected variables always converted. ordered TRUE, creates ordered factor. Default: FALSE. drop_na TRUE (default), tagged NAs converted regular NA (excluded factor levels). FALSE, tagged NAs kept factor levels label text. drop_unused TRUE, removes factor levels zero observations. Default: FALSE. add_non_labelled TRUE, values without labels included factor levels using numeric value level name. Default: FALSE (unlabelled values become NA, warning naming variables). drop.na, drop.unused, add.non.labelled Defunct dot-case argument names, removed mariposa 0.6.9. Calling function error; use snake_case equivalents instead. (formals retained old names error clearly instead swallowed ....)

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: input labelled variables converted factors. single vector input, returns factor.

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: labelled variable, numeric codes replaced associated value labels. resulting factor levels ordered original numeric values (alphabetically). Distinct codes share label text (e.g. ".." unlabelled points scale) stay distinct levels code appended: ".. (2)", ".. (3)". original code every level kept factor's "codes" attribute (named numeric vector, names = levels), to_numeric() to_labelled() can restore original values (e.g. 6, 42, 90) instead renumbering levels 1, 2, 3. attribute survives dplyr verbs (filter(), mutate(), arrange(), ...) , like variable label, dropped base subsetting (x[]) longer applies levels renamed extended.

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Perform ANOVA followed by Tukey post-hoc test anova_result <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  # Tukey post-hoc comparisons anova_result %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # With weights anova_weighted <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education, weights = sampling_weight)  anova_weighted %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Multiple variables anova_multi <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(trust_government, trust_science, group = education)  anova_multi %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #>   trust_government: 6 comparisons, 0 significant (p < .05) #>   trust_science: 6 comparisons, 0 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Grouped analysis anova_grouped <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  anova_grouped %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #> [region = East] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 2 significant (p < .05) #> [region = West] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

title: Measure Population-Representative Kurtosis — w_kurtosis
text: Uses SPSS Type 2 (sample-corrected) excess kurtosis formula. First, population excess kurtosis (\(g_2\)) calculated: \(g_2 = \frac{m_4}{m_2^2} - 3\) \(m_2 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^2 / V_1\) \(m_4 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^4 / V_1\) \(V_1 = \sum w_i\). , bias-corrected (Type 2) kurtosis : \(G_2 = \frac{(n+1) \cdot g_2 + 6}{(n-2)(n-3)} \cdot (n-1)\) \(n = V_1\) weighted data.

title: Measure Population-Representative Skewness — w_skew
text: Uses SPSS Type 2 (sample-corrected) skewness formula. First, population skewness (\(g_1\)) calculated: \(g_1 = \frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}}\) \(m_2 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^2 / V_1\) \(m_3 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^3 / V_1\) \(V_1 = \sum w_i\). , bias-corrected (Type 2) skewness : \(G_1 = g_1 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}{n-2}\) \(n = V_1\) weighted data.

title: mariposa 0.7.4 (development)
text: Accumulates changes since 0.7.3 went live CRAN (see .claude/VERSIONING_POLICY.md §5, CRAN cadence).

title: mariposa 0.7.4 (development)
text: Result objects defaults change ways existing code can notice. move mariposa closer SPSS remove silently wrong output; none deprecation bridge old values wrong misleading (VERSIONING_POLICY §4.2). maintainer decision changes ship 0.7.4 rather MINOR bump (one-exception VERSIONING_POLICY §3). One-sample t_test(): mean_diff CI now difference mean - mu SPSS’s One-Sample Test (: mean , e.g. 3.628 instead 0.628 mu = 3). tukey_test()/scheffe_test(): one row per pair SPSS’s “() - (J)” orientation every path (: "B-" unweighted, "- B" weighted), unweighted differences can change sign; new SE t_value columns. Grouped levene_test(): results carry group-key columns instead one Group string, sig column gone, values longer rounded, grouped method longer variable argument (analysis variables go ... data-frame method). w_*() results use one long format eleven functions (columns income, income_n, income_eff_n replaced Variable, statistic, n, weighted_n, effective_n, missing). Weighted describe(): N column sum weights (SPSS FREQUENCIES/DESCRIPTIVES), longer Kish’s effective n; Missing weighted. Weighted crosstab(): cell counts follow SPSS’s default /COUNT ROUND CELL (rounded cells, margins percentages rounded cells). chi_square(): correct = TRUE, Phi Cramér’s V come Pearson chi-square (SPSS Symmetric Measures); Goodman-Kruskal gamma p-value now uses SPSS’s ASE0 (wrong , e.g. .614 instead .460); gamma reported ordinal pairs; label_maps gone (tables carry labels dimnames). binomial_test(): Group 1 category first valid case data (per group), SPSS NPAR TESTS /BINOMIAL defines (: lowest code), test proportion 0.5 gives SPSS’s one-tailed exact p-value observed direction (new column alternative). , p = 0.6 test category two-tailed: p = 8e-69 instead SPSS’s .011 (reference Test 1d, now asserted). p-values come binomial tails, weights summing billions longer exhaust memory. wilcoxon_test()/pairwise_wilcoxon(): Z follows SPSS (smaller rank sum, never positive) direction new z_based_on column; Phi 2x2 table (chi_square(), phi()) signed like SPSS’s. positive SPSS prints negative value (see “SPSS parity audit”). Rank tests (mann_whitney(), kruskal_wallis(), wilcoxon_test(), friedman_test()): nominal factors error; ordered factors ranked level order everywhere. print.fisher_test() default digits 4 -> 3. Weighted linear_regression(): vcov(), confint(), nobs(), df.residual(), tidy() glance() use SPSS’s frequency-weight df (N = sum weights), matching summary (: R’s analytic-weight df, SEs CIs disagreed summary). logistic_regression(): confint() broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE) return Wald intervals (SPSS “C.. EXP(B)”); profile likelihood via confint(method = "profile"). pearson_cor(alternative = "less"/"greater") returns one-sided CI; pairwise summary table longer shows r² (still $correlations). Grouped regressions, tests scale analyses skip group computed (warning naming ) instead aborting whole call; skipped groups listed result. efa(): components/factors reflected SPSS’s sign convention (positive loading sum), signs can flip relative 0.7.3; ML compact line reports extraction variance. reliability(): item zero variance removed scale (warning), alpha changes item included; omega Heywood solution NA. ancova() “Parameter Estimates” use SPSS indicator coding last category reference (term names change); factorial_anova() ancova() stop error constant dependent variable. rec(rules = "rev") reverses scale range (valid value labels plus observed values) instead observed range; rec() returns haven_labelled vector labels exist. to_label() data frame skips metric variables whose valid values carry labels; duplicate label texts become distinct levels (“ ()”). strip_tags()/untag_na() keep value labels (labelled result); na_frequencies() reports numeric codes code order. std(), center(), pomps() to_numeric() return plain NA SPSS missing values (SPSS COMPUTE semantics). row_count(count = c(4, 5)) counts cases values (SPSS COUNT); used recycle vector. frequency() hides empty factor levels unless show_unused = TRUE. text: Single-value recode rules now match decimal codes (e.g. "3.6=2") even stored value carries floating-point representation error. single-value comparison changed exact numeric equality (x == value) string comparison (.character(x) == .character(value)), rounds 15 significant digits thereby absorbs error. Reason: value 0.1 + 0.2 stored 0.30000000000000004, previous exact == test silently failed match rule "0.3=...". mirrors behaviour sjmisc::rec(), rec()’s string syntax modelled. Range rules already robust (use >=/<=) unchanged.

title: mariposa 0.6.3.1
text: Adds explicit tidy(), glance(), augment() methods linear_regression logistic_regression results, registered via standard s3_register() pattern (broom Suggests, hard dep). Reason: class(r) = c("linear_regression", "lm"), broom::tidy.lm() broom::glance.lm() dispatched expected, internally called summary(x) — (specialised summary.linear_regression() overriding summary.lm) returned mariposa SPSS-style summary instead lm summary broom needs. visible failures: broom::glance(r) raised object 'r.squared' found mariposa’s summary stores R_squared. broom::tidy(r, conf.int = TRUE) returned 4 columns (term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) instead expected 6+ (term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high). new methods strip linear_regression / logistic_regression class delegating broom::tidy.lm / tidy.glm etc., inner summary() call dispatches summary.lm / summary.glm broom receives expected shape. user-facing summary(r) still returns mariposa’s SPSS-style output (specific method wins). Edge cases stay consistent rest lm-generic surface: broom::tidy() / glance() / augment() grouped pairwise result raise actionable error pointing lapply(r$groups, ...) use = "listwise". New tests test-broom-methods.R cover three tidiers regression types, plus grouped/pairwise error paths.

what: Behavior Change — regression results inherit from lm / glm
title: mariposa 0.6.3
text: linear_regression() logistic_regression() results now fitted lm / glm object (mariposa-specific tables attached additional slots), instead wrapping $model. base-R broom generics dispatch natively: Class hierarchy c("linear_regression", "lm") linear c("logistic_regression", "glm", "lm") logistic. summary(r) still returns SPSS-style mariposa summary (specific method wins); raw lm/glm summary call stats::summary.lm(r) / stats::summary.glm(r).
code: r <- linear_regression(survey_data, life_satisfaction ~ age + income) coef(r)                                 # named numeric vector predict(r, newdata = head(survey_data)) # works directly anova(r)                                # sequential SS table vcov(r); confint(r); residuals(r); fitted(r) broom::tidy(r); broom::glance(r); broom::augment(r)

what: linear_regression() and logistic_regression(): factor predictor handling
title: mariposa 0.6.2
text: regression functions now expose factors argument controlling factor predictors enter model. new default factors = "dummy" matches base R lm() / glm(): factor L levels expands L - 1 dummy contrasts via stats::model.matrix(). Previous versions silently coerced factor levels integer codes (SPSS ordinal--scale default) warning, surprised users relied standard R semantics. restore previous SPSS-style behavior, pass factors = "numeric" explicitly. mode emits one-line cli::cli_inform() listing coerced variables transparency. “numeric” mode required reproduce SPSS REGRESSION / LOGISTIC REGRESSION output factor predictors carry ordered meaning (e.g., 4-level education variable treated 1–4 ordinal scale). Behavioral consequences: model 3-level factor predictor previously returned one coefficient row now returns two dummy-contrast rows new default. pairwise missing handling (use = "pairwise"), factor predictors supported factors = "dummy"; function now errors actionable message pointing either factors = "numeric" use = "listwise". Migration: scripts depend old SPSS-style coercion set factors = "numeric" call site. cli_inform() message can silenced suppressMessages() desired.

title: mariposa 0.6.2
text: Two functions joined Charter §5.1 audit list (“unrounded sum(w)” weighted-statistics convention previously applied t_test, oneway_anova, levene_test): linear_regression(): weighted variance, SE, df, F, R², adjusted-R² now use unrounded sum(weights) throughout. Earlier versions used n_effective <- round(sum(w)) df MS calculations, producing systematic drift SPSS REGRESSION (~0.001 F, ~0.01 adj-R² typical weights). displayed N still round(sum(w)). logistic_regression(): pseudo-R² formulas (Cox & Snell, Nagelkerke, McFadden) now use unrounded sum(weights) exponential denominator. displayed N rounded classification counts remain integers. bug fixes; weighted results may shift slightly toward closer agreement SPSS v29.

title: mariposa 0.6.1
text: Three weighted statistical functions corrected use unrounded sum(w) per SPSS frequency-weights convention. Earlier versions rounded early produced systematic drift SPSS weighted scenarios. t_test(): weighted variance, SE, df calculations now use unrounded sum(w) (one-sample two-sample paths). Welch- Satterthwaite df now derived unrounded per-group weighted N. oneway_anova(): weighted variance divisor now (sum(w) - 1) (sample formula, population). Weighted SE uses sqrt(sum(w)), sqrt(physical n). Weighted CI t-critical-value uses df = sum(w) - 1, Kish design-effective N. df_within now uses floor(sum(w)) - k (SPSS ONEWAY-specific convention). levene_test(): weighted Levene df now uses unrounded sum(w) - k (SPSS T-TEST family convention). changes bug fixes may slightly shift weighted-scenario results user code. Differences small (typically < 0.01 F t) bring mariposa closer agreement SPSS v29.

title: mariposa 0.6.1
text: vignette("spss-compatibility") documents per-function validation status, four tolerance tiers, SPSS-procedure-specific WEIGHT conventions discovered migration: T-TEST family: unrounded sum(w) ONEWAY: floor(sum(w)) UNIANOVA: Type III SS NPAR TESTS: WEIGHT effectively ignored NONPAR CORR (Spearman, Kendall): WEIGHT effectively ignored CORRELATIONS (Pearson): WEIGHT honored CROSSTABS, FREQUENCIES, RELIABILITY, FACTOR, REGRESSION: WEIGHT honored

title: mariposa 0.6.1
text: second audit pass identified additional math defects test fudges, corrected release: dunn_test(): SE now includes Dunn (1964) / Conover (1999) tie correction. Previous versions systematically -estimated |Z| tied data (e.g., Likert scales). Baselines regenerated PMCMRplus::kwAllPairsDunnTest (exact match 4 decimals). friedman_test(): weighted branch now applies tie correction consistently stats::friedman.test (unweighted branch). inconsistency caused weighted chi-squared values low tied data. describe(): weighted skewness kurtosis now delegate .calc_skewness() / .calc_kurtosis() helpers.R (Joanes-Gill Type-2 Σw substitution), matching w_skew() / w_kurtosis() SPSS FREQUENCIES exactly. previous duplicate implementation used simple weighted moment without bias correction. .w_quantile(): weighted quantiles now use Type-6 (HAVERAGE) linear interpolation cumulative-weight crossings — matches SPSS FREQUENCIES /PERCENTILES. Unweighted quantiles also switched R default type = 7 SPSS-compatible type = 6.

title: mariposa 0.6.1
text: Several SPSS-compatibility claims narrowed reflect code actually : Source comments test-file headers weighted paths kruskal_wallis(), wilcoxon_test(), friedman_test() corrected “design-based” / “Lumley-Scott” “frequency-weighted approximation”. mann_whitney() genuine Lumley & Scott (2013) implementation; others substitute sum(w) n standard variance formula. mann_whitney() test now includes permanent cross-check survey::svyranktest() (skipped survey installed). spearman_rho(): weights parameter docstring rewritten disclose weights used case filtering (per SPSS NONPAR CORR convention), rank correlation . pearson_cor(): docstring now warns weighted-df convention (n = sum(w)) gives spuriously narrow CIs raw expansion weights; users weights normalize first. logistic_regression(): test file replaced property-based assertions (Wald formula, Sig chi-sq, exp(B) vs independent 2x2 odds ratio, Cox & Snell/Nagelkerke/McFadden textbook formulas, Omnibus likelihood ratio). longer tautological glm-vs-glm self-comparison.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: release adds 10 label management functions working labelled survey data (inspired sjlabelled, consolidated clean, consistent API), plus data transformation, row operations, data exploration functions.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: New var_label(): dual-mode function getting setting variable labels. var_label(data) returns variable labels named character vector; var_label(data, x = "Age", y = "Gender") sets labels specific columns. Supports tidyselect column selection getting labels. New val_labels(): dual-mode function getting setting value labels. val_labels(data) returns value labels named list; val_labels(data, x = c("Low" = 1, "High" = 2)) sets labels. Use .add = TRUE extend existing labels without replacing . New copy_labels(): copies label attributes (variable labels, value labels, class, tagged NA metadata) source data frame matching columns target. Essential preserving labels dplyr operations strip attributes. New drop_labels(): removes value labels values actually occur data. Use drop.na = TRUE also remove labels tagged NA values.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: New to_label(): converts haven_labelled vectors factors, using value labels factor levels. Supports ordered, drop.na, drop.unused, add.non.labelled options. Factor levels ordered original numeric codes (alphabetically). New to_character(): converts haven_labelled vectors character, replacing numeric codes label text. New to_numeric(): converts factors labelled vectors numeric. use.labels = TRUE, uses value labels numeric; otherwise assigns sequential integers (controlled start.). New to_labelled(): converts factors, character, numeric vectors haven_labelled proper value labels. Factor levels become value labels automatically.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: New set_na(): declares specific numeric values missing (NA tagged NA). Supports unnamed values (applied numeric columns) named pairs per-variable control (e.g., set_na(data, income = c(-9, -8))). tag = TRUE (default), creates tagged NAs integrate na_frequencies(), frequency(), codebook(). Can called incrementally add new missing value codes. New unlabel(): strips label metadata variables, converting haven_labelled vectors plain base R types. Removes variable labels, value labels, tagged NA metadata, format attributes. Tagged NAs become regular NA. Supports tidyselect selective column unlabelling.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: New rec(): flexible recoding string syntax (e.g., rec(data, x, rec = "1:2=1 [Low]; 3:5=2 [High]")). Supports value ranges, min/max keywords, copy unchanged values, automatic value label generation bracket syntax. Works numeric, character, labelled vectors. New to_dummy(): creates dummy (indicator) variables categorical labelled vectors. Generates one 0/1 column per unique value informative column names. Supports tidyselect multi-variable dummy coding suffix = "label" use value labels column names. New std(): z-standardization four methods ("sd", "2sd", "mad", "gmd"). Supports survey weights, grouped standardization via dplyr::group_by(), robust = TRUE median/MAD-based standardization. New center(): mean-centering (grand-mean group-mean). Supports survey weights dplyr::group_by() group-mean centering. Returns centered values centering value stored attribute.

title: mariposa 0.6.0
text: New row_means(): computes row-wise means across selected columns, min_valid parameter matching SPSS MEAN.x() syntax. Designed use inside dplyr::mutate(). Replaces deprecated scale_index(). New row_sums(): computes row-wise sums across selected columns, min_valid parameter minimum valid (non-NA) values. New row_count(): counts occurrences specific values per row. Useful counting endorsements multi-item scales (e.g., many items respondent agreed ).

title: mariposa 0.4.0
text: Added fisher_test() Fisher’s exact test independence contingency tables. Recommended sample sizes small expected cell frequencies fall 5 (chi-square approximation becomes unreliable). Supports survey weights, multi-variable analysis, group_by(). Added chisq_gof() chi-square goodness--fit testing. Tests whether observed frequency distribution categorical variable matches expected distribution (default: equal proportions). Supports custom expected proportions, residual analysis, survey weights, multi-variable analysis. Added mcnemar_test() testing changes paired proportions two dichotomous measurements (e.g., /designs). Provides asymptotic exact binomial p-values, 2×2 contingency tables, continuity correction. Supports survey weights. Added dunn_test() S3 generic Dunn’s post-hoc pairwise comparisons following significant Kruskal-Wallis test. Identifies specific group pairs differ using rank-based Z-statistics adjustable p-value correction (Bonferroni, Holm, BH, etc.). Dispatches kruskal_wallis result objects. Added pairwise_wilcoxon() S3 generic pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons following significant Friedman test. Identifies measurement pairs differ adjustable p-value correction. Dispatches friedman_test result objects.

title: mariposa 0.3.1

Like Oblimin, Promax oblique rotation produces Pattern Matrix, Structure Matrix, Factor Correlation Matrix. Uses stats::promax() (base R, new dependency). title: mariposa 0.3.0

Includes rank categories (negative, positive, ties) effect size r. Added friedman_test() comparing 3+ related measurements ordinal data (non-parametric alternative repeated-measures ANOVA). Effect size: Kendall’s W. Added binomial_test() testing whether observed proportion matches expected value (exact binomial test). Supports multiple binary variables custom test proportions.

title: mariposa 0.1.0
text: Refactored 9 11 w_* functions use shared factory pattern (R/w_factory.R). Eliminated ~2,460 lines duplicated boilerplate (4,204 → 1,740 lines, -58.6%). w_modus w_quantile remain standalone due fundamentally different interfaces. Added 83 SPSS validation tests w_* functions across 4 scenarios (weighted/unweighted × grouped/ungrouped) test-weighted-statistics-spss-validation.R. Reduced memory usage: result objects now store columns needed post-hoc tests instead full input data frame. Unified print helper system: output formatting now uses print_helpers.R. Removed deprecated .print_header(), .print_border(), .get_border(), .print_group_header() helpers.R. Deduplicated t_test.R print methods: print.t_test_results print.t_test_result now share common implementation (~360 fewer lines). Added input validation: t_test(): validates conf.level 0 1 t_test(), oneway_anova(): validate selected variables numeric chi_square(): warns expected cell counts < 5 Migrated error handling stop()/warning() cli_abort()/cli_warn() structured messages, {.arg} {.var} markup, pluralization support. Added cli dependency professional user-facing messages print output. Added @family tags 24 exported functions cross-referencing documentation (families: descriptive, hypothesis_tests, correlation, posthoc, weighted_statistics). Added tests/testthat/helper-mariposa.R shared test utilities centralized SPSS validation tolerances. Migrated print_helpers.R infrastructure cli (cli_rule(), cli_bullets(), cli_h2()). Extended globals.R missing NSE variable declarations. Fixed “SURVEYSTAT” reference imports.R.
